name: Drafting a Manuscript
title: Drafting a Manuscript
answer: Drafting a manuscript is the stage of research writing where findings, methods and prior work are assembled into a single document intended for peer review and publication. It covers the choice of venue, the structure of the paper, the writing of each section, and the preparation of figures, tables and references. In an AI research context it also covers reporting model details, datasets, training procedures and evaluation results clearly enough for another researcher to reproduce or assess the work.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Drafting a manuscript is the stage of research writing where findings, methods and prior work are assembled into a single document intended for peer review and publication. It covers the choice of venue, the structure of the paper, the writing of each section, and the preparation of figures, tables and references. In an AI research context it also covers reporting model details, datasets, training procedures and evaluation results clearly enough for another researcher to reproduce or assess the work.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on a reference manager for citations, a typesetting system such as LaTeX or a word processor with a template from the target venue, and a version control or backup habit so drafts are not lost.Figures are usually produced in a plotting tool and exported in a vector format the venue accepts.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The usual method is to fix the claim and the evidence before writing prose, then draft sections in an order that suits the author, often methods and results first and introduction and abstract last. Each claim in the draft should trace to a result, a citation or an experiment, and citations should point to the original paper rather than to a secondary summary. Co authors then revise in rounds, and the final pass checks that the abstract, figures and conclusions agree with the numbers actually reported.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk centre on authorship, plagiarism, duplicate submission and the correct attribution of data, code and prior text. Venues require disclosure of conflicts of interest, funding, and any use of generative tools in producing the text, and most treat the human authors as fully responsible for the content regardless of how it was drafted. Provenance matters for every reused figure, dataset or quotation, and permissions are needed where a figure is reproduced from another source. This is a description of common practice, not legal advice.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Drafting is moving toward tighter reporting standards for models and data, wider sharing of code and artefacts alongside the paper, and clearer rules on how generative tools may be used and disclosed. Reviewers increasingly expect claims to be checkable against released materials, which pushes authors to write methods and limitations with that scrutiny in mind. The direction is toward manuscripts that function as a reproducible record rather than a standalone narrative.
sections.heading: Where it is going
